title: Third Circuit rules AI training on copyrighted material is not fair use — first federal appeals decision
subtitle: A unanimous appeals panel affirmed Thomson Reuters' summary judgment against Ross Intelligence over Westlaw headnotes, setting the first binding circuit-level precedent on the question that every active AI copyright suit is fighting over.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit on September 29 affirmed a lower-court grant of summary judgment to Thomson Reuters in its 2020 copyright suit against Ross Intelligence. The ruling, now digested across legal and AI press into early October, holds that Ross's use of thousands of Westlaw headnotes — short editorial summaries of legal holdings — to train a competing legal AI search engine was not fair use. It is the first federal appeals court decision on AI training as fair use. The panel found that Ross's use was commercial, substituted for a licensable product, and used the headnotes as more than a stepping stone to an unprotectable idea. The case now returns to the Delaware district court for damages.

The reasoning is narrower than the headline suggests, and that narrowness is where the fight continues. The Third Circuit emphasized three facts specific to Ross: the training data was copied from a direct competitor's commercial product, Thomson Reuters offered a licensing market Ross declined, and the output was engineered to compete in the same market. Courts in the Bartz v. Anthropic litigation and in the NYT v. OpenAI case have reached partially different conclusions on parallel questions — most notably that training on legally obtained books can be fair use even when storing pirated copies is not. The Third Circuit opinion threads around rather than directly contradicts those decisions, but it hardens the law on competitor-to-competitor training.

This matters for every active AI copyright suit because the discovery and litigation calculus just shifted. Plaintiffs now have a circuit-level precedent to cite. Model developers who scraped from direct competitors — code training on competitor codebases, legal AI training on competitor case summaries, news-aggregation AI training on competitor articles — are in materially worse legal position than they were a week ago. The ruling does not settle the general question of whether all AI training is fair use, but it closes off the strongest defense in the competitive-substitution subset of cases. Expect settlement conversations in half a dozen pending suits to intensify.

For learners who want to understand AI and copyright at the level that will actually matter in your career: read the opinion itself. It is 60-odd pages and it walks through all four fair-use factors applied to AI training with more precision than any secondary source. Then compare it to Judge Alsup's Bartz v. Anthropic ruling. The two together are the current state of the law, and they will be the baseline every future ruling cites. Secondary coverage is a starting point; the primary texts are what practice is built on.
